entry: City, capital of Miyagi Prefecture and the largest city in the Tōhoku region of Japan (pop., 2023: 1,098,335). Founded in 1600 by the *daimyō* Date Masamune, who ordered construction of Sendai Castle and a surrounding castle town on a grid plan, the city is nicknamed the City of Trees for its zelkova-lined avenues. Its Tanabata festival, held each summer, is the largest in Japan, and in winter thousands of lights decorate the trees for the Pageant of Starlight. A railway to Tokyo opened in 1887, and in 1925 the Senseki Line became the first underground railway segment in Japan. On March 11, 2011, a magnitude 9.0 offshore [[Earthquake|earthquake]] triggered a destructive [[Tsunami|tsunami]] that devastated the coast.

Roman Stoic philosopher, statesman and dramatist. Born in Corduba in Hispania and trained in rhetoric and philosophy in Greece, Seneca wrote 12 essays and 124 letters on moral issues, which constitute one of the most important bodies of primary material for ancient [[Stoicism]]. His plays, all tragedies, include *Medea*, *Thyestes* and *Phaedra*. Exiled to [[Corsica]] in AD 41 under Emperor [[Claudius]], he was allowed back in 49 to tutor [[Nero]]. When Nero became emperor in 54, Seneca became his adviser and, with the praetorian prefect Sextus Afranius Burrus, provided competent government for the first five years of the reign. His influence declined, and in 65 he was forced to commit suicide for alleged complicity in the Pisonian conspiracy against Nero. His calm death became the subject of many paintings. During the [[Renaissance]] he was regarded as a master of literary style and a model of dramatic art.

Country on the Atlantic coast of West Africa; capital, [[Dakar]]. Senegal nearly surrounds [[The Gambia|Gambia]], which occupies a narrow strip along the Gambia River, and it borders [[Mauritania]], [[Mali]] and [[Guinea]]. Its name derives from the [[Senegal River]]. The state formed as part of the independence of French West Africa from colonial rule, and it has been a semi-presidential republic since its foundation in 1960. French is the official language but is understood by only a small minority; Wolof, spoken by about 80% of the population as a first or second language, is the lingua franca. Over 30 languages are spoken, and Senegalese people are predominantly Muslim. Most people live on the coast and work in agriculture or food industries. Senegal is a heavily indebted poor country, ranking 169th of 193 on the [[Human Development Index|Human Development Index]]. It is a member of the [[African Union]] and the United Nations.

River in West Africa, 1,086 km long, forming much of the border between Senegal and Mauritania. Its headwaters, the Bafing and Bakoye rivers, rise in Guinea and join at Bafoulabé in Mali. The river drains a basin of 270,000 km² and has a mean flow of 680 m³/s. It flows west and then north past Kayes and Podor before entering the Atlantic Ocean, separated from the sea by a thin sandbar called the Langue de Barbarie. In 1972 Mali, Mauritania and Senegal founded the Organisation pour la mise en valeur du fleuve Sénégal (OMVS) to manage the basin; Guinea joined in 2005. Two large [[Dam|dams]] regulate the river: the Manantali Dam in Mali and the Maka-Diama Dam near the mouth, which keeps salt water from moving upstream. As of 2012 the river carried very little commercial traffic, and a proposed navigable channel would give landlocked Mali a route to the Atlantic.

Period of almost continuous civil war and social upheaval in [[Japan]] during the 15th and 16th centuries. The Ōnin War (1467) is commonly chosen as its start, while proposed end dates range from 1568 to 1638. It overlapped the Muromachi period (1336–1573) and saw the decline of the Ashikaga shogunate as regional lords, or *daimyō*, gained power. Warriors from humble backgrounds could rise to become [[Samurai|samurai]] and then daimyō; [[Toyotomi Hideyoshi]], born to a peasant family, became a samurai, daimyō and kampaku, or imperial regent. Modern Japan honors [[Oda Nobunaga]], Hideyoshi and [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]] as the "three great unifiers" who restored central government.

Novel by English author [[Jane Austen]], published anonymously in 1811. Austen's debut had the working title *Elinor and Marianne*. It follows the three Dashwood sisters and their widowed mother after they are forced to leave their family estate in Sussex for a cottage in [[Devon]]. Elinor embodies sense through restraint and duty, while Marianne represents sensibility through emotional intensity, and the sisters' romances test their contrasting characters. Austen critiques the excesses of romantic sentimentality. Ang Lee directed a 1995 film adaptation.

Special sense through which odors, or smells, are perceived. In humans, an odor binds to a receptor in the nasal cavity and sends a signal through the [[Olfactory system|olfactory system]] to the olfactory bulb, where glomeruli aggregate the signals for identification, memory and emotion. Smell helps detect food, hazards and [[Pheromone|pheromones]] and contributes to [[Taste|taste]]; retronasal smell plays the biggest role in flavor. Mammals have about a thousand genes for odor reception, but humans have far fewer active odor receptor genes than other primates. Linda B. Buck and Richard Axel, who cloned olfactory receptor proteins, were awarded the [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prize]] in 2004. Competing theories of odor coding remain, and no theory fully explains olfactory perception. Anosmia, or loss of smell, may result from nasal congestion, infections, traumatic brain injury or neurodegenerative disease.

Device that measures a physical quantity and converts it into an electrical signal. Sensors detect events or changes in their environment and send the information to other electronics, frequently a computer processor. Analog sensors such as potentiometers and force-sensing resistors remain widely used in manufacturing, aerospace, cars and medicine. A sensor's sensitivity is how much its output changes when the measured input changes; a thermometer whose mercury moves 1 cm per 1 °C has a sensitivity of 1 cm/°C. Sensors should be sensitive to the measured property, insensitive to others, and have little effect on what they measure. Microsensors made with MEMS technology are often faster and more sensitive than larger devices. Optical sensors measure [[Refractive index|refractive index]], and electrochemical sensors monitor [[PH|pH]] of fluids. An analog output must be converted with an analog-to-digital converter before digital use.

Part of the nervous system responsible for processing sensory information. A sensory system consists of sensory neurons, including receptor cells, neural pathways and parts of the [[Brain|brain]] involved in perception. Commonly recognized systems serve vision, hearing, touch, taste, smell, balance and visceral sensation. Receptors are commonly grouped as chemoreceptors, photoreceptors, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors; each converts its stimulus into an electrical action potential that travels along afferent neurons. Gautama Buddha and [[Aristotle]] classified five traditional human senses: touch, taste, smell, vision and hearing. Pain, balance and temperature are also well accepted in most [[Mammal|mammals]], and some animals possess magnetoreception and electroreception. The receptive field is the area of the body or environment to which a receptor responds.

Unit of language expressing a complete thought, typically with a subject and predicate. In traditional grammar a sentence is a string of words that expresses a thought; in functional linguistics it is a unit of written text delimited by capital letters and punctuation such as periods, question marks and exclamation marks. A sentence can express a statement, question, exclamation, request, command or suggestion. By clause structure, a simple sentence has one independent [[Clause|clause]], a compound sentence has two or more, a complex sentence adds at least one dependent clause, and a compound-complex sentence combines both. Sentences are also classified by their [[Speech act|speech act]], such as assertion, question or command.

Indigenous people of North Sentinel Island in the [[Bay of Bengal]]. Along with the Great Andamanese, Jarawas, Onge, Shompen and Nicobarese, they are one of six indigenous peoples of the [[Andaman and Nicobar Islands]]. They have had minimal contact with outsiders and have usually been hostile to those who approach the island. Designated a particularly vulnerable tribal group, they live as [[Hunter-gatherer|hunter-gatherers]]. India declared the island a tribal reserve in 1956, prohibits travel within 5 km of it, and maintains an armed patrol in the surrounding waters. Estimates of the population range from 50 to 200 individuals, with wider estimates up to 500.

14th monarch of the [[Joseon]] dynasty, reigning 1567–1608. Born Yi Yeon, the third son of Prince Deokheung, he succeeded King Myeongjong, who died young without an heir. Early in his reign Seonjo appointed Confucian scholars, including Yi I and Yu Sŏngnyong, reformed the civil service examination to stress politics and history, and restored the reputations of executed scholars. His court then split into rival Westerner and Easterner factions, a two-faction system that lasted some 200 years. Japanese forces under [[Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] invaded Joseon in the [[Imjin War|Imjin War]] (1592–1598). Seonjo fled the capital, Hanseong (today [[Seoul]]), and appealed to Ming China for military aid. He is remembered for political discord and incompetent leadership during the war.

Capital and largest city of [[South Korea]], on the Han River in the northwest of the Korean Peninsula. Its population peaked above 10 million and stood at about 9.6 million in 2024; the wider metropolitan area, with Gyeonggi Province and Incheon, holds more than half of South Korea's population. The Baekje kingdom founded the settlement in 18 BC, and the [[Joseon]] dynasty later made it the capital, surrounded by a fortress wall. The [[Empire of Japan]] occupied the city in the early 20th century. The [[Korean War]] saw it change hands four times and left it largely in ruins, but rapid reconstruction followed. Seoul hosted the 1988 Summer Olympics and the 2010 G20 summit, and five [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] World Heritage Sites lie within the Seoul Capital Area. In 2004 the Constitutional Court declared that Seoul must remain the national capital unless a nationwide referendum changes this, although Sejong City hosted 10 of the government's 18 ministries as of 2019.

Principle dividing a state's government into distinct branches, usually legislation, execution and adjudication. Each function must be conceptually and institutionally distinct, so that each branch maintains its integrity. The principle is closely linked to checks and balances, in which branches limit one another. Separation of judicial power from the other branches is the norm in modern democracies. Many countries, however, fuse legislative and [[Executive (government)|executive]] powers, notably parliamentary systems on the Westminster model, where parliament is supreme. Separation of executive and legislative powers is the main principle of presidential systems. [[John Locke]] articulated the idea in *Two Treatises of Government* (1689), and [[Montesquieu]] refined it in *The Spirit of the Laws* (1748). The U.S. Constitution vests legislative power in Congress, executive power in the president and judicial power in federal courts, with vetoes and appointments serving as checks.

Life-threatening condition, also called septicemia, in which the body's dysregulated response to [[Infection|infection]] injures its own tissues and organs. Symptoms include fever, rapid heart rate, rapid breathing and confusion. Septic shock is low blood pressure that persists after fluid replacement. Bacteria are the most common cause, though viruses, parasites and fungi also cause sepsis. Treatment requires immediate intravenous fluids and [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]], often in an intensive care unit. Sepsis affected about 49 million people in 2017 and caused 11 million deaths, about one in five deaths worldwide. The risk of death is as high as 30%, and as high as 80% in septic shock.

Coordinated suicide attacks by [[Al-Qaeda|al-Qaeda]] against the United States on September 11, 2001. Nineteen hijackers seized four commercial airliners. Two were flown into the Twin Towers of the [[World Trade Center (1973–2001)|World Trade Center]] in New York City, one struck the [[The Pentagon|Pentagon]] in Arlington County, Virginia, and the fourth crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers revolted. The towers collapsed within an hour and 42 minutes of being struck. The attacks killed 2,977 people and caused at least US$10 billion in infrastructure and property damage. The United States invaded Afghanistan and launched a [[War on terror|global war on terror]], and [[NATO]] invoked Article 5 of its treaty for the only time to date. [[Osama bin Laden]] was killed in a U.S. raid in Abbottabad, Pakistan, in May 2011. Other countries tightened airport security and strengthened anti-terrorism laws. One World Trade Center, begun in 2006, opened on the site in 2014.

Ninth month of the year in the [[Gregorian calendar|Gregorian]] and Julian calendars, with 30 days. In the Northern Hemisphere it marks the beginning of meteorological autumn, and in the Southern Hemisphere, of spring. It begins the ecclesiastical year in the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]] and the academic year in many northern countries. The name comes from Latin *septem*, "seven", because September was the seventh month of the oldest known Roman calendar before January and February were added. The September equinox falls in this month. In the United States, September is the third most common birth month.

Earliest surviving Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, abbreviated LXX. According to a legend in the Letter of Aristeas, seventy-two Jewish translators, six from each of the twelve tribes of Israel, were commissioned by [[Ptolemaic Kingdom|Ptolemy II Philadelphus]] to translate the Torah into Greek. Some scholars consider the story pseudepigraphical, but the first five books are dated with confidence to the mid- or late 3rd century BCE, probably translated in [[Alexandria]], and the remaining books to the 2nd century BCE. Koine Greek and Aramaic were the [[Lingua franca|lingua francas]] of Second Temple Jews, and few could read Hebrew, so the translation served Jewish communities. Early Christians used it as their [[Old Testament|Old Testament]], and it is directly quoted about 300 times in the New Testament.

Brazilian [[Heavy metal music|heavy metal]] band from [[Belo Horizonte]], formed in 1984 by brothers Max and Igor Cavalera. The band was a major force in groove metal, thrash metal and death metal from the late 1980s to the mid-1990s. Its second album, *Schizophrenia* (1987), drew the attention of Roadrunner Records. *Beneath the Remains* (1989), *Arise* (1991), *Chaos A.D.* (1993) and *Roots* (1996) made it one of the most popular bands in heavy metal history, selling almost 20 million units worldwide. Max Cavalera left in 1996 and Igor in 2006. In March 2024 the band began a two-year farewell tour, after which it disbanded.

Ordered list of elements, finite or infinite, in which the same element may recur at different positions. Unlike a [[Set (mathematics)|set]], order matters: (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8) is a valid sequence. The length of a finite sequence is its number of elements, and each element's index is its position, usually counted from 0 or 1. In analysis the nth term is often written *aₙ*. The [[Fibonacci sequence|Fibonacci sequence]], in which each term is the sum of the previous two, is a classic example. Sequences are the basis for [[Series (mathematics)|series]] and are used to study convergence and [[Limit of a sequence|limits]]. In computing, finite sequences are usually called strings, words or lists, and infinite sequences are called streams.

Species of coniferous tree native to groves on the western slopes of California's [[Sierra Nevada]]. Also called the giant sequoia, giant redwood or Sierra redwood, it belongs to the subfamily [[Sequoioideae|Sequoioideae]] and is among the largest trees on Earth. Trees typically grow 50–85 m tall, with trunks 6–8 m in diameter. The oldest known specimen is 3,200–3,266 years old, making it one of the oldest living organisms. Its wood is fibrous and brittle and unsuitable for construction. The IUCN lists the species as endangered, with fewer than 80,000 remaining in its native California.

Subfamily of coniferous trees, known as redwoods, in the cypress family Cupressaceae. It includes the largest and tallest trees in the world, which can live for thousands of years. Three living species are known: the coast redwood (*Sequoia sempervirens*), the [[Sequoiadendron giganteum|giant redwood]] and the dawn redwood (*Metasequoia glyptostroboides*). The coast redwood and giant redwood are native to the western United States, while the dawn redwood is native to [[China]]. The subfamily reached its peak of diversity in the early [[Cenozoic]]. Sequoia and Sequoiadendron are massive evergreens; Metasequoia is deciduous, much smaller, and can live in colder climates. Threats include logging, fire suppression and burl poaching. Most modern phylogenies place Sequoia as sister to Sequoiadendron.

Cherokee polymath and creator of the Cherokee syllabary. Also known as George Gist or George Guess, Sequoyah was a neographer, a creator of new writing systems, of the Cherokee Nation. In 1821 he completed the syllabary, which enabled reading and writing in the Cherokee language. The Cherokee Nation adopted it in 1825, and within a quarter-century its literacy rate reached almost 100%, surpassing that of surrounding European-American settlers. His creation is among the few times a member of a pre-literate group invented an original, effective [[Writing system|writing system]], and it is believed to have inspired 21 scripts used in 65 languages in North America, Africa and Asia. He also represented the Cherokee in Washington, D.C., where he signed two relocation-and-land-trading treaties. Few primary documents describe his life.

Celestial being originating in ancient Judaism and a type of [[Angel|angel]] in Abrahamic religions. The Hebrew word *saraph* means "burning". In the [[Hebrew Bible]] book of Isaiah, seraphim are six-winged beings that fly around God's throne crying "holy, holy, holy"; this scene profoundly influenced later theology, literature and art. Seraphim are also mentioned in the Book of Enoch and the [[Book of Revelation|Book of Revelation]]. Tradition places them in the highest rank of Christian angelology and the fifth of ten ranks in the Jewish angelic hierarchy. In Islam, seraphim are referenced in hadith as throne-bearers.

Landlocked country in Southeastern and Central Europe; capital, [[Belgrade]]. Serbia has about 6.5 million inhabitants and borders Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro. The Serbian Kingdom was established in 1217 and reached its territorial peak in 1346 as the Serbian Empire. The [[Ottoman Empire]] annexed the territory by the mid-16th century. Serbia gained international recognition of its independence in 1878 and became a kingdom in 1882. In 1918 it joined the Croats and Slovenes to form the Kingdom of [[Yugoslavia]], and after World War II it became one of six federal units of socialist Yugoslavia. In 2008 [[Kosovo]] declared independence, which Serbia regards as part of its sovereign territory. Serbia is a parliamentary republic and an upper-middle-income economy negotiating accession to the [[European Union]].
